question: A 3-year-old child with long-standing cholestasis and chronic fat malabsorption develops progressive ataxia and areflexia. Vitamin E levels are undetectable. Which management approach is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Standard oral preparations are not absorbed in fat-malabsorption states. A water-soluble form is required to bypass biliary insufficiency.

answers.text: Water-soluble form of Vitamin E (alpha-tocopheryl polyethylene glycol succinate, TPGS) at high dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In cholestasis and fat-malabsorption, conventional fat-soluble Vitamin E is not absorbed. TPGS (water-miscible Vitamin E) at doses of 15–25 IU/kg/day is absorbed independent of bile salts and is the correct choice.
Incorrect. IM Vitamin E preparations are not routinely available and are not first-line. Water-soluble oral TPGS is the established approach for fat-malabsorption-associated deficiency.

answers.text: High-dose oral vitamin C as a compensatory antioxidant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Vitamin C does not substitute for Vitamin E in membrane antioxidant protection. The deficiency must be directly corrected with absorbable Vitamin E.

overallFeedback.feedback: In fat-malabsorption states, standard fat-soluble Vitamin E is not absorbed. The correct approach is a water-soluble form (TPGS) that is absorbed without bile-salt-dependent micelle formation.
Correct. Water-soluble Vitamin E (TPGS) is the treatment of choice when fat malabsorption prevents absorption of conventional preparations.
